q: Why are some languages considered "dead" while others are just dormant?
What is the difference between dead and dormant languages?
a: A language is considered 'dead' when it no longer has any native speakers — people who learned it as their first language from birth. This is different from a 'dormant' or 'sleeping' language, which has no native speakers but is still maintained by a community that uses it for specific purposes like religious ceremonies, education, or cultural preservation. A language is 'extinct' when it has no speakers at all, not even second-language learners. The distinction between dead and dormant is important: dead languages like Latin, Ancient Greek, and Sanskrit are studied academically and used in specific contexts but have no native speakers. Dormant languages like Hebrew (before its revival) or Cornish have communities working to revive them. Language death occurs when a community shifts to a more dominant language, usually due to factors like colonization, globalization, urbanization, or government policies. UNESCO estimates that half of the world's 7,000 languages will disappear by the end of the 21st century. Efforts to preserve and revive languages include documentation, education programs, and digital resources.

A language is 'extinct' when it has no speakers at all. Language death occurs when communities shift to dominant languages due to colonization, globalization, or government policies.
